title: How the bug-watcher watches (local folder, and who has a compiler)
desc: How the bug-watcher watches. It doesn't see keystrokes — it watches your LOCAL folder (where edits are saved), not GitHub (only updates on push) and not the Graphify map (an after-the-fact snapshot). It skips .git, target, venvs, graphify-out and its own reports so it can't loop; waits for saving to settle (debounce reduces but can't eliminate half-finished checks), drops any stale check if you save again, then runs build/lint/test once on the newest snapshot; the debugger only steps in for a crash or freeze. Compilers: Rust is strict; Go also compiles (lighter, but flags unused imports); Python only compiles to bytecode (syntax), so the watcher adds ruff (names) and mypy (types). A compiler only catches misspelled code identifiers — a wrong filename, config key, API field, or DB column looks valid and still needs a test, type, or schema.

title: The bug-watcher CLI — how it works
desc: A reusable command-line “watcher” that catches bugs on its own across Rust, Go, and Python. Point it at the run or test command you already use (cargo test, go test, pytest); it watches for a crash, a failed test, or a freeze (a timer catches hangs and grabs a stack snapshot). It saves what it can — the error output, the exact failing test, any seed or input it reports — then does a best-effort replay under the right debugger (CodeLLDB for Rust, with plain LLDB as the fallback; Delve/dlv for Go; pdb/debugpy for Python), pausing where it fails. It will not catch silent wrong answers; those still need a test or check that defines “right”. One command, same steps for all three: watcher -- <your command>.

title: Your AI's memory + catching bugs by itself

Crashes and failed tests get caught automatically the moment they happen; silent wrong answers need a rule (a test, assertion, or sanitizer) that defines 'right'. The loop is detect, capture the clues, then replay under the debugger.

title: Who is the independent reviewer?
desc: You got confused by a word — I wrote 'seat', not 'sheet'. A seat is just a job in the team: one worker, one chair, one job. Some seats plan, some build, one reviews. The plan seat is Full SDD — it writes the detailed plan (the blueprint) that says what each piece should do. Other seats (Feature Tickets + Green Pass) write the actual code, following the plan. So who reviews? The plan seat: at the end someone checks 'does the code match the plan?', and the best judge is Full SDD — it wrote the plan (knows it cold) but didn't write the code, so it's honest, not marking its own homework. That's what 'independent' means. Like a house: the architect draws the blueprint, builders build it, then the architect walks through and asks 'does this match my blueprint?' — knows the plan, didn't lay the bricks, perfect judge. The manager is the boss: it does NOT read the code itself, it just hands the code to Full SDD and won't let anything move forward until the check passes — that's all 'owns the gate' means. Plainly: a robot (Greptile) scores if the code is tidy, the Full SDD seat says if it matches the plan, the manager makes sure both happen, and nobody checks their own work.

title: Greptile just gives a score
desc: You asked what Greptile actually is: a robot that reads a pull request and gives it a score out of 5 — that number is its whole job, it doesn't judge whether the work is right. That 5/5 is the Clean? half of the gate (tidy, up to standard). The 12 'code smells' are NOT Greptile's list — they're what Feature Tickets cleans its own code against before the PR; Greptile just scores what comes out. The other half is Right? — does the code do exactly what the ticket asked — and that goes to the Full SDD seat (it wrote the plan but not the code, so it's a real outside opinion), with the manager handing it the diff and enforcing the answer. A PR only auto-merges to staging if both pass; a Right? fail sends it back even at a perfect 5/5. The worker never grades itself — Feature Tickets only gives its own change a quick glance, never the sign-off. And it's not live yet: it's all written in two pull requests (#29 the rulebook, #39 the tool), switched on only after you approve the merges and the setup re-runs.

title: Can a "weaker" checker judge a "stronger" worker?
desc: Your model-power worry: the manager (the checker) runs on a model you rate below the feature-ticket worker's, so can a less powerful checker really judge a more powerful worker's code? Two reasons it's smaller than it looks. First, checking is easier than cooking: the reviewer isn't re-writing the code, it just reads the finished work and asks 'does this match what the ticket ordered?' — you don't need to be a chef to tell the plate isn't what you asked for, and matching to a written order is far easier than making it. Second, the hard parts go elsewhere anyway: 'is the code any good?' goes to a specialist robot (Greptile), not these models; 'does it actually work?' goes to the tests and the Tester seat later; only 'does it match the ticket?' is left — the easy slice, guarded on both sides. What you decided: B — the manager still owns and enforces the gate, but hands the actual read to the Full SDD seat, same model tier as the worker, which wrote the plan but didn't write this code. Equal muscle, deepest plan knowledge, still independent.

title: When the clock turns on
desc: The clock has a gate — it doesn't tick all day. It runs only when 2+ teams have live work (an idea has come in and the manager has started handing it out); fewer than two and it's off. Teams flip it on: the second a manager takes an idea and starts assigning work, it pings me 'Received an idea — start your clock', and it pings 'idle/done — stand down' when the pipeline ends. Once two are live I start the clock and it only checks in with the teams actually working — idle teams are left alone (they'd have no idea what I meant, and something has to be active first). Below two busy teams it switches off on its own. Right now it's off on purpose: all three teams are idle. Kick an idea to two teams and it comes alive by itself — nothing for you to switch. The rule is saved to GitHub and passed to every manager (DMS writes it up for the rest).

title: Who checks it, and when?
desc: Once each — one independent review, and why. The first pass in the loop is really a tidy, not a review: after the code goes green, Feature Tickets cleans its own code, and only it can because that means editing code and the manager never codes — so that stays with the worker. The second pass is the real review of the finished change, asking two questions: Clean? (tidy, no smells) and Right? (does what the ticket asked) — this is the one that must be independent. Clean? goes to the robot (Greptile), which doesn't care who wrote the code. Right? goes to the Full SDD seat: it wrote the plan but not this code, so it's a real outside opinion — the manager owns and enforces this gate (routes the diff, holds the merge on a fail), with Feature Tickets keeping just a quick sanity glance first. One check, not two: two looks by the same eyes minutes apart is the exact redundancy we just killed on the worker; the real review happens once, at the gate, by seats that didn't write the code. Free bonus: the manager is already at the promotion-to-main gate with you, so if the robot's fixes changed the code it has Full SDD re-check 'still matches the ticket?' there at no extra cost. The setup: once each — Full SDD does the one real Right? check, the robot does Clean?, plus the free re-peek at the gate.

title: Should a worker grade their own homework?
desc: The weak spot you spotted: right now the same worker (Feature Tickets) writes the code, cleans it, and checks it — twice. That's marking your own homework, and it quietly undoes the loop's own trick of splitting the test-writer from the pass-maker so nobody clears their own bar. One honest checker already exists: the robot reviewer (Greptile) at the gate doesn't care who wrote the code, so it fairly judges 'is it clean?' — but it doesn't know what the ticket was meant to do. So the real gap is 'did it do what the ticket asked?', which needs someone who knows the ticket but didn't write the code. Your one decision: who owns that check — (1) the manager (already verifies + guards the plan, knows the ticket, never codes; a little more manager time per batch), (2) another teammate cross-checks (keeps it off the manager, but they have a stake and it muddies their one job), or (3) nobody, robot only (simplest, but 'did it match the ticket?' goes unchecked by anyone independent). I'd pick the manager.

title: How your teams check in
desc: The reporting rhythm in plain English. The day is 3 work blocks in your time — Block 1 9am–1pm, Block 2 2–5pm, Block 3 6–8pm. Before each block a 'spaceship' note (8:45am, 1:45pm, 5:45pm) says what got done since work last stopped; the 8:45 one is the morning check-in. At each block's end (1pm, 5pm, 8pm) a wrap-up says what can keep going without you. Between blocks, an hourly heartbeat: each team sends one line — what changed or 'nothing changed' — so a stuck team is caught within the hour, not hours later; you never see these. You only get pinged once 2+ teams have something inside a 30-minute window, never one team alone, and nobody sits idle — wait 30 minutes, carry on. Plus the ping-back rule: an agent pings the moment a job is done and never goes quiet; if a ping I'm owed doesn't land in ~1 hour I chase it, and I never trust 'done' on someone's word — I check it myself. One decision: the clock that fires all this is off — start it on the work-block schedule, or leave it off. I'd start it.

title: How our TDD loop works now
desc: The whole build loop in plain English, with the new review rules folded in. Two workers on purpose: Feature Tickets writes the test + cleans the code + owns the PR; Green Pass only makes it pass — you can't game a test you didn't write. Per ticket: RED (Feature Tickets writes an honest failing test first — checks inputs/outputs not the guts, no cheat-tests) → GREEN (Green Pass makes it really pass, smallest change, no faking) → REFACTOR (Feature Tickets tidies its own code against a fixed list of 12 'code smells' — cleanup #1, in the loop). Before the PR, Feature Tickets gives its own diff a quick sanity glance — but it doesn't grade its own work. THE GATE checks two axes independently — the robot (Greptile) judges Clean? (the 12 smells), and the manager hands Right? (does exactly what the ticket asked) to the Full SDD seat, which wrote the spec but not this code. Batch up to 5 tickets; both axes must pass to auto-merge to staging — a Right?-fail returns the PR even at Greptile 5/5. Otherwise → 7 tries, still stuck → split into smaller PRs, each with its own fresh 7 tries, only a still-stuck split comes to you (more tries, or merge as-is). Only you promote staging → main, with a passing test + your yes. Cleanup happens both in the loop and at the gate; the test stays honest from the first red.

title: Who actually does the code review?
desc: I took the portable parts of Matt Pocock's code-review method and wired them into the build loop. Two new rules: a two-way check on every change (Clean? — against a fixed list of 12 'code smells'; Right? — does exactly what the ticket asked, no more) and honest tests (no fake pass, no peeking at insides, no test that breaks on tidy-up). Your catch: a rule everyone can see is nobody's job — the rulebook reached all 10 seats as background but told no worker it was theirs. Fixed by making the review independent and giving each part an owner: Feature Tickets (honest reds, clean against the smells, a sanity glance only — it doesn't grade its own work) and Green Pass (make it really pass, no faking), with the check split at the gate — Greptile judges Clean?, the Full SDD seat (via the manager) judges Right?, since it wrote the spec but not the code. Tester and Front-end left out for now. All in 2 pull requests, not merged — your yes needed. Two decisions for you: keep clean-up in both build+review or move to review only; and whether to wire the other 2 seats.

desc: The plain-English version of how a brand-new team starts using the template. The template is a 'starter kit' — a set of empty folders, one per job, with blanks that say <TEAM> where the name goes. One command does the rest: it makes a fresh private notebook just for that team, photocopies the starter kit into it (one folder per job — manager, the two planners, researcher, tester, and the rest), writes the real team name into every <TEAM> blank, adds a shared handoff tray for half-finished tasks, saves and uploads the notebook to the team's own private place online, then checks its own homework and stops loudly if any blank was left empty. The big thing to understand: it's a photocopy, not a live feed — the team gets a snapshot of the template exactly as it looks the moment they're created, and after that they work from their own copy. Change the template later and that team doesn't automatically get it; someone has to hand them an update. (The folders mostly hold sticky-notes pointing to the shared rulebook, not the rules themselves — those come down a separate pipe.)

title: How it all works now (the map)
desc: The whole system in one map, top to bottom — and the fix to a common mix-up: an idea does NOT start with Ops. 1) Your idea goes straight from you to the core Manager, one-on-one, never through Ops; the whole planning stage is just you and the manager. 2) Get set up to plan: together you pick the language, name the repo, decide what's needed, Research prices it, and you approve the cost + setup before any planning starts. 3) The plan gets written and approved: two planners draft it (blind, then merged) through two Plannotator checkpoints with Wayfinder between; you approve the facts then the plan at each — four approvals — giving the Gold Plan + PRD. 4) Cut into sections: the approved plan splits into as many sections as it needs (no limit), each section a department; one section needs no department, the core team builds it. 5) Three crews at a time: only 3 teams run at once (core + 2), the rest queue, one out one in. 6) NOW Ops is the switchboard: while teams build, reports and day-to-day decisions go team → Ops → you and back (planning always stays direct). 7) It all comes together: each piece rolls up team → central staging → main into one codebase (main needs your OK), and a rule change reaches everyone when you tell Ops 'push'.

title: Who inherits what?
desc: When a team starts — or gets updated — 'inherit' hides a split. Three separate things travel at different speeds. RULES: a rule change reaches a new team AND the running teams (SM, HAP) automatically — that's the refresh, on your word. TOOLKIT + CODE: a brand-new team is built from the shared master copy, so it gets every tool and every bit of code finished so far; but SM and HAP copied the toolkit when they started, so new tools built later do NOT reach them on their own — someone has to pull them in (no background robot does it). PRIVATE NOTES: never travel — each team keeps its own private notebook, a new team starts empty and fresh, nobody inherits another team's notes. One decision inside: should toolkit updates auto-reach running teams too, or stay a deliberate manual pull? (I lean manual for now — rules are safe to auto-send, code isn't.)
